content_metadata.description: This video provides an informative demonstration on dissecting and examining the female genitalia of the South American Cactus Moth, focusing on the dissection procedure and anatomical analysis.

qAndA.question: What color is the Eosin stain used in the video?

qAndA.answer: Two pairs of forceps are used.
qAndA.question: How many pairs of forceps are used to separate the ventral and dorsal sides of the abdomen?

qAndA.answer: Chlorazol Black is used to stain the membranes of the genitalia.
qAndA.question: What is the purpose of dipping the genitalia in Chlorazol Black?

qAndA.answer: The presence of the spermatophore remnants in the corpus bursa indicates that the female has mated.
qAndA.question: How can you tell if a female Cactus Moth has mated?

qAndA.answer: Cactoblastis cactorum has a prominent signum, while Melitara prodenialis either lacks a signum or has a very small, reduced one.
qAndA.question: How does the signum of Cactoblastis cactorum differ from that of Melitara prodenialis?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: The South American cactus moth has been introduced into the United States and now ranges along
the coast from South Carolina to Louisiana.
It remains a threat to prick the pair of cactus and the desert ecosystem the Southwestern
United States and Mexico.
In a previous video we demonstrated the dissection and slide mounting of the male genitalia for
making identifications of the cactus moth.
Here we demonstrate the dissection of the female which has some modifications to the method
from that use for the male.
In our previous video of the male we discussed the tools, supplies and reagents needed for
making dissections and slide mounts.
We also demonstrated the method for removing the abdomen for placing two a vial of potassium
hydroxide for softening overnight.
After the female abdomen is removed from potassium hydroxide it is transferred 20% ethanol
for initial cleaning.
We tamp and brush the abdomen from the posterior end to the open end to your end to remove
the inner contents.
We brush the abdomen to further remove many of the scales.
After most of the scales are removed the abdomen and genitalia are transferred to eosinstein
where they remain for 3-4 hours.
After staining the abdomen is transferred to 70% ethanol where it is further cleaned the
abdomen is brushed from side to side to minimize tearing of the inner segmental membranes.
After the abdomen is cleaned two pairs of forcipes are used to separate the ventral
sternites from the dorsal turguides.
Staining at the open end of the abdomen the ventral and dorsal sides are gently torn
apart all the way to the last abdominal segment just before the ovaposter.
At that point between the 7th and 8th segments the inner segmental membrane is torn across
the sternum and then later torn across the dorsal.
The inner segmental membrane is torn the genitalia can be removed.
The digestive tract another extraneous material can now be easily removed taking care not
to damage the globular corpus bursa and the connecting ductus bursa.
The abdomen and genitalia can be dipped into chlorosol black for a few seconds to stain
the membranes.
Then the genitalia is washed in 70% ethanol to remove the excess stain.
The abdomen and genitalia are given a final cleaning before being placed under glass
chips in 100% ethanol for positioning the parts and hardening.
The slide is made with the same method used for the male desections and labeled accordingly.
Here we can see the structures of the female genitalia including the papilianalis or ovaposter
pads, the apophysies for muscle connections, the osteoom or opening for insemination which
leads into the ductus bursa and the corpus bursa where the spermatifor is stored after
mating.
Whether or not the female has made it can be determined by presence of the remains of
the spermatifor in the corpus bursa.
The form of the speratized signal can be used to differentiate some species.
Here we can see the female genitalia of cactoblastis on the left and the native melatera prudinialis
on the right.
Species of melatera either lack a signal or have a very small reduced signal compared
to the one in cactoblastis.

youtube_description: This video describes tools, supplies, and techniques for dissecting the female genitalia of the cactus moth, Cactoblastis cactorum.  Structures of the genitalia can be used to differentiate Cactoblastis cactorum from other species of cactus feeding moths. The cactus moth is native to South America, but has been used as a biological control agent in Australian and other areas to control introduced species of prickly pear cactus. This moth was first detected in the Florida Keys in 1989.  It has since spread northward on the Atlantic Coast to South Carolina and westward on the Gulf Coast.  In 2008 it was detected on the coastal islands of Mississippi, and in 2009 in was detected in Jefferson Parish, Louisiana. This species is an imminent threat to native cactus and the desert ecosystem in southwestern United States as well as to cultivated cactus in Mexico.
